initial_requirements: The Oregon University System wants to update the Get Real website to encourage high-school students to consider computer science degrees and careers. The site should provide a teen-friendly path through university course information, career guidance, stories from computing professionals, and practical preparation advice. It should serve both students already interested in computing and college-bound students who may need more context or encouragement.

slots.key: CMS/platform selection criteria
slots.value: Compatibility with the university’s existing platform or environment should be a priority. The CMS should fit the current hosting and security environment, work with existing user login or permission setups if needed, support the university’s design and accessibility standards, and integrate cleanly with existing analytics, media hosting, and course information sources. It should support secure hosting, regular updates, role-based access control, and use the university’s existing staff single sign-on approach rather than requiring a separate CMS account system. Identity management details should be confirmed with the university IT team, including whether all campuses or units use the same sign-in method or whether there are exceptions. It should provide analytics for site improvement, and pull in or link to existing content sources without a lot of manual re-entry. Hard-to-secure, hard-to-maintain, or difficult-to-access environments are a concern. Security review should be built into the environment, accessibility support should be consistent rather than optional, controlled integration with other systems is preferred, and sign-in integration is probably only needed for editors and approvers, not for students browsing the site, pending confirmation with the technical team.

slots.key: Legal caution on outcome claims
slots.value: Avoid claims that sound like guarantees, especially around careers, admissions, or outcomes. Present student stories and graduate outcomes as examples, one person’s path, or one possible result—not promises that everyone who follows the path will get the same career or admission outcome. Use safer, persuasive phrasing like “this can lead to” or “students may explore,” while still being specific about skills, preparation, and opportunities. If a story is unusual, still in progress, or depends on a very specific opportunity, make that clear right in the story so students don’t assume it’s the normal path. Even for more typical stories, a light qualifier can help, especially when the example could be mistaken for a guarantee or a standard outcome. In general, avoid absolute claims like guaranteed job placement, guaranteed admission, or “everyone can do this if they try.” If a story or outcome is sensitive, add a plain-language disclosure that it’s an example, not a promise, and make sure wording is accessible and easy to understand for teens and families.

slots.key: Definition of a successful student-facing experience
slots.value: Welcoming, simple, and not too academic right away; teens should immediately understand it is a low-pressure place to explore computer science, with a clean first screen that avoids clutter and jargon and guides them to one or two obvious next steps, such as learning what CS is, hearing from real people, or finding out how to prepare. The site should let curious teens start here and then gradually offer more detail as they choose to dig deeper. It should also let students jump straight to the most relevant section if they already know what they want, while still connecting curiosity, preparation, and careers and making it easy to move naturally to the next step from any section. Success would mostly mean a visitor gets from the teen-friendly intro content into the more substantive course or career information, and spends enough time there to actually engage with it. If they also move on to related pages like preparation advice or stories, that’s a good sign the site is helping them explore. A weaker path would be one where people arrive, bounce quickly, or stop at a general page without getting to anything that explains why computer science might matter to them. We are not necessarily expecting an application or sign-up action right away, since this site is more about interest and guidance.

slots.key: Key project risks that could affect launch or adoption
Prioritization rules for batching, speeding up, or deferring updates
slots.value: Use impact and urgency as the main filters. Changes that affect deadlines, broken links, inaccurate course information, or anything a student could act on right away should move faster. Minor polish items and small wording improvements can wait for the next batch. When staffing is tight, bundle non-urgent updates into scheduled review windows. Low-value, duplicative, or likely-to-change-again-soon items should be deferred rather than processed immediately. Truly urgent cases are those where delaying would mislead students, cause them to miss an important deadline, or leave them with broken or outdated information that affects their next step. Examples include changed course offerings, admissions deadlines, and serious factual corrections. If an item is only helpful to have sooner but not harmful to wait, it should stay in the normal batch; the key test is whether delay creates real student impact versus minor inconvenience.

slots.key: Final approver fallback and escalation handling
slots.value: If the issue changes more than just wording or small content details, especially if it affects accessibility compliance, legal sensitivity, or whether the page can publish on time, it should escalate. If the editor or backup can reasonably fix it with clear comments, it should go back for revision. Escalation is also appropriate if the approver and contributor are stuck in a loop and need higher-level judgment to resolve it.

revisions.new_value: If the final approver is unavailable, the issue should be reassigned to a backup approver so work does not stall. If the final approver disagrees, the issue should be documented and either sent to a higher-level owner or brought back with clear guidance on what needs to change. There should always be a fallback path for time-sensitive updates.
